strengths: SFTMix addresses a relevant NLP problem with a straightforward adaptation of hidden-state Mixup to instruction tuning. Its confidence estimation uses existing training data without requiring additional human annotation or proprietary-model scoring.

Table 1 reports consistent improvements across seven model–dataset configurations spanning three model families. Gains over NTP are approximately 0.20–0.40 MT-Bench points and 0.32–1.67 percentage points in length-controlled AlpacaEval-2 win rate.

The medical experiments provide complementary evidence through objective accuracy measurements: average improvements are 1.33 and 1.66 percentage points for Llama and Mistral. Human evaluation also favors SFTMix, with 42.5% wins versus 26.5% losses across 200 judgments.

Experiments with LoRA, data selection, smaller reference models, and multilingual tuning demonstrate useful practical flexibility. The transfer of the selected hyperparameters to other model–dataset settings strengthens the empirical contribution.
weaknesses: The central claim that confidence-based pairing is crucial is not adequately isolated. There is no comparison against ordinary random-pair Mixup on the same dataset, or confidence estimated from a single checkpoint. Section 5.2 changes the response dataset and tests quality-based pairing without a confidence-based comparator on that modified dataset. It therefore does not establish that training dynamics explain the gains over generic Mixup.

Evaluation leaves material uncertainty. Appendix A.1 selects hyperparameters using the same MT-Bench and AlpacaEval-2 scores subsequently reported, without identifying a separate validation set. Five evaluation rounds do not establish robustness across independent training runs, and confidence intervals or paired significance analyses are absent. These issues particularly affect interpretation of the smaller gains and ablation differences.

The proposed mechanism is stronger than the supporting analysis. Separation in a t-SNE visualization and a 7% reduction in training-confidence standard deviation do not demonstrate reduced overfitting or improved generalization specifically among low-confidence examples. Section 3.4 establishes that Mixup changes gradients, which holds independently of confidence-based pairing. Held-out analyses stratified by confidence would provide more direct evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful optimizer and epoch specifications. The manuscript does not adequately specify reference-checkpoint scheduling, sequence-length limits and formatting, LoRA configuration, or exact generation and judge settings, and it provides no implementation link. Human evaluation omits annotator counts, assignment details, and agreement estimates. The cross-entropy signs in Sections 3.1 and 3.3 also conflict with the convention used in Section 3.4.

The broader comparative contribution needs clearer support. Prior cartography-based Mixup is cited but insufficiently differentiated, and relevant simple regularization alternatives are not experimentally compared. Reference-model training and checkpoint scoring add substantial work, but total computational overhead is not quantified. The weaker-reference experiment is promising, although it does not establish the overall performance–cost tradeoff. The missing isolating controls and evaluation/reproducibility details keep the otherwise promising contribution borderline for Findings.
